452.t: Why he left: monopoly over his outside work and fear for his wife
452.s: Cobb explains he left because Hampton and Gladys wanted every booking to come through them, and he took a witness because he feared the notice would be denied.
452.ch: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
452.q: So I said, 'Well, you go so far and -- of course, I had saved me some money, and I would go on and form my own band; not form my own band, to play this job, I was forming a band for the two weeks I had in Philadelphia (inaudible). And I was determined mostly to go after I found out that they wanted…

452.t: Deciding to leave Hampton in 1947 and planning to rest
452.s: After a Pittsburgh Courier night at Carnegie Hall, Cobb resolves to leave, using his back as an excuse, after the Wantz brothers book him for Easter and Gladys objects that it didn't come through her.
452.q: Yeah. I tell you what -- I played a Pittsburgh Courier thing at Carnegie Hall with him at midnight and we received awards, and I was in the running of the saxophone players for the Pittsburgh Courier. And, of course, we had to stay up until 8:00 o'clock that morning going into Columbus, and this is…

452.t: Handing in his notice in Cleveland with a detective as witness
452.s: In Cleveland Cobb gives Hampton written notice with a detective friend present as witness and plays one show before Johnny Griffin takes over.
452.ch: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
452.q: (Inaudible) another hour at the RKO. I had a friend there that, a very good friend of mine that was a sergeant, plain clothes detective, and everybody thought we was brothers. His name was Harry. And the day that I brought him up to the theater, I told (inaudible). So we met up in Hamp's dressing…

1.t: Bennie Payne, the pianist who begged for his job
1.s: Pianist Bennie Payne belittled Barker's lack of solos, then had to beg to be rehired after army service, which Barker contrasts with his own quitting in 1946.
1.q: Plunger and effects. Dizzy’s going out to outer space, and they couldn’t understand that, so they had to scuffle. That was it. I stayed there, and the word begin to get around. Bennie Payne, the piano player . . . I walked in the dressing room. We had been friendly, been out together. Said, “Hey,…

1.t: Quitting Cab Calloway after a twenty-dollar fine
1.s: Danny says he missed a show at the Paramount, was fined twenty dollars when others were not, and quit, wanting to work with his wife Lu.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: Yeah. They had tears coming out. It's a shock. You know, you were with Cab... Because it's a stigma on your career. You'all been fired. But he didn't fire me. I just left. Because I was late and missed a show. And he damn near cried when I left, I don't know for what reason. He said, "Why are you…

504.s: He wanted a change and more freedom, as Miles wanted more specific grooves from the drums.
504.ch: Joining and playing with Miles Davis
504.q: I think it was ‘70. Because Ndugu Leon Chancler went to Europe with Miles and the band had Don Alias and Keith and Gary Bartz. When they came back from the summer, Miles called me. They had a few more gigs. Did New York City, maybe one or two other gigs and then I left. I just wanted a change of…

504.t: Why he left Charles Lloyd and the quartet's discography
504.s: He left because he wanted to play other music; they review Lloyd records, including one with Tony Williams.
504.ch: New York and the Lloyd quartet
504.q: Yes, Of course, Of Course. A lot of people don’t know about that record with Gabor and Ron. Nice record.

505.t: Leaving Miles in Brazil to lead his own band
505.s: He left because he had Lookout Farm and a band in waiting; Miles asked about his plans and Liebman gave notice in Brazil.
505.q: It wasn’t that bad. It wasn’t so bad. That guy, Azar, he didn’t know what to do. I felt bad for him. He didn’t know what to do. But it was near the end, because – the reason I left him, which is because I had a band in waiting. I had done already Lookout Farm with ECM and was about to do Drum Ode,…

505.t: Ending Lookout Farm and wanting guitar and more composed form
505.s: He explains letting Beirach go solo and wanting guitar and written form after the Chick tour.
505.ch: The Scofield-Hino quintet and return to New York
505.q: Yes. I was ready for guitar. I had had enough piano. Also, another reason – I should backtrack that I broke Lookout Farm up because I wanted to do this project with Pee Wee. The way that I painted it, it was commercial. We had – I just want on the record that it was positive. It was a good project.…

92.t: Leaving Tatum to join Nat Cole
92.s: Collins worked again with Tatum, then Nat Cole called; Tatum reluctantly let him go and he stayed about fourteen years until Cole died.
92.ch: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
92.q: So Art was going into some club on the east side, I can't think of it now, and he wanted me to play with him. So I promised him that I would so Slam was with him and I went with Art again. I worked with Art for quite a while and I got this call from Nat Cole to come with him. Well, I was under…

92.t: Tatum's reluctance to see Collins leave for Nat Cole
92.s: Tatum was under contract to Collins and unhappy that he left in St. Paul to join Nat at the Tiffany Club, but came to hear them nightly.
92.ch: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
92.q: But any way, I wondered about it. I left him in St. Paul, Minnesota. I flew to California and joined Nat at the Tiffany Club, and I wondered how Art really felt about it. I knew he was a little peeved with me, and with Nat, but as soon as he came to California I looked up at night and there he was…

385.t: Low man on the Tatum pole; the agent who broke up the trio
385.s: He struggled to keep up with Tatum, practicing at intermission; an agent convinced Tatum to go solo and the trio ended.
385.ch: California, Cats and the Fiddle, the Tatum trio
385.q: I loved to go fishin'. I used to make a little light living crabb'in and cookin' crabs, sellin' papers, shinin' shoes, I did everything....

385.t: How the Tatum trio broke up
385.s: An agent persuaded Tatum to work alone; Grimes was away, later running into Tatum in Canada while with the Highlanders.
385.ch: Three Deuces and 52nd Street with Tatum
385.q: The only thing I can remember about that was we were workin' I think still at the 3 Deuces -- back again. We were in and out of there. And it was said that there would be a vacation -- we weren't gonna work for four or eight weeks or somethin'. That sounded funny 'cause we were in demand, you know.…

19.t: Lucky Thompson quits and Dexter Gordon comes in; route to Boston
19.s: Lucky leaves in Boston because he cannot stand the band's behavior, and Dexter Gordon replaces him.
19.q: But anyway, to get ahead of the story a little... About Lucky Thompson. Later we played Boston, Massachusetts, and Lucky just went to Billy Eckstine and told him, "Look, I've had enough of this. I can't stand it any more. These guys are doing everything" and so-and-so-and-so. So Lucky quit the…

19.t: Leaving Eckstine in September 1945 to study, and forming a trio
19.s: Convinced he must stop and learn more, he leaves despite Eckstine's protest and forms a Nat Cole-style trio with Tommy Potter and Chester Brown.
19.ch: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
19.q: And Sarah was replaced by a girl named Ann Sawyer, a very fine vocalist. The last time I saw her, she had married and had a club in West Virginia. Ann Sawyer came in, and different guys were beginning to leave the band. So by this time, I was thoroughly convinced that I was in an entirely new and…

179.t: Red Allen goes north; Bocage joins Kid Thomas and later stops playing
179.s: Allen met King Oliver and asked Bocage whether to go; Bocage declined to follow, played with Kid Thomas a couple of years, then quit about twenty years ago.
179.ch: Excelsior Brass Band and Red Allen's band
179.q: Well, John stayed with the band until Allen went off. Like I said, you see, when Allen first left, yeah, Allen met with King Oliver, you see,

172.t: The Silver Leaf band and who replaced Ridgley
172.s: Ridgley does not recall who replaced him on trombone in the Silver Leaf band. It broke up after he and Celestin left.
172.q: Silver Leaf. Yeah. I don't know who they did get to play trombone after I left them. Silver Leaf after we organized our home. I think the band kind of went to pieces after that. Because Celestine and I both left, you see. I don't think they ever got that band together anymore. But Albert Battista.…

626.t: Leaving and rejoining the band; the last three survivors
626.s: He briefly left the band, came back, and names Johnny Pope, himself and Denny Trainor as the old players still alive.
626.q: Yeah, I left the band for a while. I left the band for a while. They made me a band for some instance, and I quit for a while, but they insisted on me coming back and I went back, you see. I wondered too about in the... I stayed in it until I just got tired and went down, going down, so I just…

83.t: Banashak losing Allen Toussaint to Marshall Sehorn
83.s: While Toussaint was in service Banashak worked to keep him an artist, then Sehorn won him as partner, leaving Banashak feeling betrayed.
83.q: Yeah. Well, when he came back, Marshall got him to go be with him, be his partner with him, with Marshall, as opposed to Joe. And I think he felt that that was done in an unfair manner. I don't know whether it was or wasn't, to be honest with you.

121.s: Ridgley demanded a release from Ruffino, leaving Johnny Adams; he left around Ruffino's 1962 death and hopes to regain his Rick songs after 27 years.
121.q: Okay. Here's how I ended my relationship with Rick. You see, Joe and I were pretty good buddies. We were friends. I was one of the artists who would go up there and meet him and talk all day about the business, even though he wasn't fair with the money. But I still liked him and I guess he liked me…

632.t: Celestin, Sharkey and George Lewis unphotographed; losing interest in Sharkey's band
632.s: He did not photograph Celestin, Sharkey or George Lewis on Bourbon Street. He first heard Sharkey's band in 1947 but lost interest once they played the same things nightly.
632.q: manuscript did you no I never did and of course I also I also didn't photograph Celestan or his other band at a couple of private functions that that I went to because I was I guess because I was there on a social basis rather than to take pictures yeah and and shock you was down Bourbon Street…

636.t: Frank Johnson's change of style and Polites resigns in 1956
636.s: Frank Traynor replaced Dyer, but Johnson moved toward a mainstream style under Armstrong's influence and Polites and others resigned by the end of 1956.
636.q: It, uh, did continue, um, using, uh, quite a good trombone player, Frank Traynor, uh, on trombone. But, um, by this time, um, Frank Johnson's, uh, uh, idea was, uh, changing. He was, uh, under the bad influence, unfortunately, of, uh, Louis Armstrong. He was one of the first, uh, jazzmen we heard…

977.t: Accompanying Bechet and leaving the Luter band
977.s: He played concerts accompanying Sidney Bechet, then left Luter's band to paint, fearing he could not keep up.
977.q: I played a few times with Bechet, because it was in 1949. 1948 and 1949. I played in concert with Claude Lutheur, accompanying Bechet. But at that time, it was too much music to me to play every day. And we played at that time, the afternoon, the night, and sometimes the morning to rehearse and to…

831.t: The Triangle Band and the Majana brothers
831.s: He played trombone in the Majana brothers' spot-job Triangle Band, quit after a dispute, and talk turns to Sato and Steve Woodrow's wife.
831.ch: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
831.q: Yeah, that was strictly a spot job band. That was two Majana brothers, Sato and Tony Majana. And I played trombone with them for a while, then Leon Mello went in, took my place when I quit them. I quit them, we had a little run in about, I went after a job and I got the job and the first night on…

203.t: Leaving Shaw and returning after Louis Armstrong records
203.s: The recording-date argument, eight months at home, and rejoining Shaw in Boston.
203.ch: Biagini, Duke and the Shaw band
203.q: Well in a way I’m glad I didn’t. You know, because the way it turned out it was good. And you get mad — I got mad at Artie. He had a recording date and this was in the 1937 band, September. And I’d been in that band too. But after the union card thing, I was not too friendly. So he had one of those…

315.t: Dave's reasons for leaving the road and the final concert, then Gerry Mulligan
315.s: Dave wanted time with his kids and finances allowed it; after the last concert George Wein got him together with Gerry Mulligan, Alan Dawson and Jack Six.
315.q: But it’s also interesting to note, and if I have my history right, that after he broke up the group and their last concert was in Pittsburgh, and I remember being impressed seeing John Chancellor from the NBC Nightly News, that was the button on the national newscast, the Dave Brubeck Quartet gave…

436.t: Trying Les Brown, then Miller band; why musicians left bands
436.s: Pete quickly leaves Les Brown for musical reasons, joins Tex Beneke's Miller band, and discusses why players changed bands often.
436.q: I remember like in ’48 I remember joining Tex Benecke in the Miller band, because Goz says, “Come on the band,” you know, “you’ve got to come on the band.” So I did that. Well before that I was back on the west coast and I joined Les Brown and went the Rich’s Garden was the first gig and we were…

539.s: Dorn explains his exit from Atlantic: his own behavior, interference after the Flack, Midler and Hathaway hits, friction with Wexler and Ahmet, and Nesuhi's absence.
539.q: Well first of all I was a wise ass kid and I was high most of the time so I didn’t exactly comport myself the way somebody should. Secondly I had had a lot of success and nobody bothered with me while I was making jazz records for Nesuhi. When I started to get hits with Flack and Midler and Donny…

656.t: Leaving Maynard Ferguson; Eric Traub's nickname
656.s: Refused a move from baritone, he gave notice; Eric Traub's nickname Zembo Mosque is recounted.
656.ch: Big breaks: New Wave, Maynard, Tony Bennett
656.q: there Migs left — Migliore left, and I asked if I could move to the alto chair and he wanted me on bari so he said no, and then Eric Traub left and I asked if I could move to the tenor chair and he said no I want to keep you on bari. That was the last straw.

349.t: Giving notice to Hampton after eighteen years
349.s: He told Hampton at the Port Authority he was quitting to follow his wife's wish; Hampton laughed it off and pressured him for months.
349.q: No. Well I’ll tell you, I worked with that man 18 years, 18 long God damn days man, or years, I worked with him. And I remember we came from overseas, we had been on a trip like Germany, Switzerland, I can’t remember some of the other places right now. But anyway, we came back and I think we were…

930.t: Leaving the band to teach at North Seattle Community College
930.s: Radke analysed Harry's appeal, then decided to go home; Gina left the choice to him, and Harry offered an open return.
930.q: And well I’ll get to that in a second. But so I’m sitting on the band. The reason I left the band, I had an offer from a friend of mine to start the jazz department at North Seattle Community College, a brand new college. And I’m sitting there. And when I joined Harry I thought, you know everybody…

494.s: The rhythm section changed, an electric bassist unsettled the band, and he gave notice exactly four years after starting.
494.ch: Dizzy Gillespie, Yusef Lateef and 1960s New York
494.q: No. For the first three years, anyway, it was the same. And like I said, we worked a lot. It sounded like a big band almost, because it was so tight. Then, my last year there, both Chris White and Rudy Collins left. I stayed. The band became – it was different. We hired an electric bass player who…

153.t: Leaving Duke for Pearl; Don Redman
153.s: He left Ellington in early 1953 to be Pearl Bailey's musical director, working with bandleader Don Redman.
153.ch: Ellington years, Pearl Bailey and Jazz at the Philharmonic
153.q: Meeting Pearl. Because I couldn’t do both. When she was busy doing her things, and I became the musical conductor for her – and I had Don Redman as the bandleader. There’s a name. There was another genius. Him and Benny Carter wrote most of the tunes for Pearl. Don Redman. Again, there was a tiny…

133.t: Leaving Blakey for the Five Spot; Lee Morgan, fines for lateness
133.s: Tired of traveling, Walton and Reggie Workman left to join a trio at the Five Spot; he adds how Blakey fined him for being late at the Apollo and said the music grew sophisticated with this band.
133.q: Oh, I got it in my head that I was just tired of traveling. Me and uh, by this time it was Reggie Workman, we left to take a long-term engagement in uh The Five Spot, which uh clubs had long-term engagements in those days. You know, we, uh, we had a trio there uh which was led by uh Tootie Heath…

371.t: Leaving JATP over its circus atmosphere
371.s: After about four and a half years, Jones left JATP because showmanship overtook the music.
371.q: In to 1951. I started in 1947… Perhaps the end of 1950. It was about four years. I guess it was about four and half years.

111.t: McCoy Tyner leaving Coltrane; Elvin's departure from San Francisco
111.s: He says he did not discuss his plans, thought Alice's wish to play may have prompted McCoy, then flew to Europe.
111.ch: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
111.q: I don’t know. I didn’t discuss my business with anybody. I don’t know…cause first of all Alice wanted to play, so that might have been good reason for McC0y to leave. She was, after all, closer to him than McCoy (Laughs). She’d say, “Honey, I want to play tomorrow.” (Laughs)

114.t: Why he left Dizzy after eight years
114.s: Playing the same set every night had grown stale, though leaving Dizzy was hard; Baker raises Las Vegas and they take a break.
114.q: Well, I guess, it was -- I guess -- I guess, yeah, because I just wanted to, I guess, maybe do something else. You know.

109.t: Leaving the Ella band to return to Minton's
109.s: With Barefield and Dizzy gone and the band too old and falling apart, he went back to Minton's; Garvin Bushell is praised in passing.
109.ch: Ella, Charlie Christian and Europe with Hayes
109.q: Yeah. Chauncey was a nice guy. He was a wonderful guy. But I just couldn't stay because, you know, I didn't figure I would be progressing, you know.

229.s: He quit in July 1949, exhausted and frustrated by Ory's repetitive New Orleans repertoire.
229.ch: C.L. Burke and Kid Ory years
229.q: I was kind of exhausted, kind of frustrated because I didn't like Ory's style of playing. The music he was playing was very monotonous, playing the same old New Orleans tunes night

65.t: Being fired by Maria Teresa Vera
65.s: After two years Vera dismissed him because he rehearsed with a radio quartet and she thought he would quit.
65.ch: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
65.q: Because I - ah - there was a kind of misunderstanding because I was rehearsing with a quartet to broadcast and she thought that I was going to leave, so she was two or three steps ahead of me in her way of thinking and she just gave me the notice.

26.t: Why he left the band in 1950 and Norman Granz's version
26.s: Greer says he left because of his wife, not Granz, and describes the small group while Duke was in Europe.
26.ch: Leaving the band, Strayhorn and reflections
26.q: Right. My wife was (unintelligible), you know. So it was a toss up between I stay with my wife and the band. Naturally, I stayed with my wife. We were good friends until he died. You know, Duke -- I didn't have to ask Duke for no money. Duke was never -- there's one word I say for Duke, the word…

677.s: Brown insists leaders do let people go, and they discuss Lil Greenwood and Jimmy Hamilton leaving over doubling pay.
677.ch: Europe 1933, New York Cotton Club, Hodges group
677.q: There may not be many, but there have been people fired. Oh well, you say I'm sorry -- I can't keep you on -- I can't keep you -- well that's firing.

9.t: Quitting Cootie Williams after his usher girlfriend's challenge
9.s: Embarrassed that his girlfriend had never heard him solo, Holmes asked Cootie for a feature; Cootie said nobody wanted to hear him, and Holmes walked out.
9.ch: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
9.q: : Well, the show come back... Oh, they come back into the Savoy for the summer, because Cootie had gone in the Savoy with the band, you know. So at that time, I was goin' with a little girl, I can say it now, that was a waitress...not a waitress, an usher in the theatre. She had never heard me play…

106.t: How the Harlemites broke up and Freddy went to Holland
106.s: The band lasted about six months for the recordings and Pleyel, then the players refused to leave their jobs; Johnson took another group to The Hague and Pete du Conge threw him out of Bricktop's.
106.q: Well, we stayed together for -- just to make those recordings, 'cause after, after we finished the recordings, that's when we were supposed to go on the road.

409.t: Duke arranged Cootie's departure to Goodman
409.s: When Goodman approached him Cootie told Duke, who set up the deal and later told him he was too big to come back.
409.ch: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
409.q: Well, the first time I was contacted by Goodman, I told him about it. I told Duke about it. And we used to go out and talk, talk about it, so he would tell me what to tell him the next time he called. And he set up the deal for me.

379.t: Quitting Cab Calloway over a humiliation
379.s: After exhausting theater runs and Cab's rehearsal demands, an incident leads him to give notice and leave without his fare.
379.q: So they start getting on my nerves the guys in the (inaudible). So one day -- we'd been traveling now for 20 -- we'd been doing 20 week of theaters. We used to do a whole lot of theater. You know, 20 week of theater would run anybody crazy. We used to do five, four, five shows a day.

167.t: Why he stayed with the Spirits and then left after the Buffalo fight
167.s: Bookings and a pact to stick together kept him until the fighting and the Buffalo clash with Doug made him quit.
167.ch: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
167.q: On account of we'd be arguing, fighting. And when that started, I got disgusted. And when me and Doug had it, and he was the leader guitar -- tipple player, him and I got in a fight in --

69.s: He was back with Duke almost three years until Willie and Louie left; Rose sorts out the timing against their move house.
69.ch: Harry James, Bellson and the return to Duke
69.q: I think you were back with Duke for quite awhile there, after you went back the second time, Juan.

641.t: Being fired by Ory after a vacation
641.s: Back from vacation, Joe found Bob McCracken in his place, was handed a notice because of friction with Ory's wife Barbara, and quit; Harvey Brooks was let go soon after.
641.ch: Joe Liggins and back to Kid Ory
641.q: Well, what happened, I went on a vacation. And like I said, I never got along with Barbara, that girl. She was still.. He left his wife for her, and he married Barbara. And when I took off, the first night I got back on the job Bob McCracken was working in my place. So Ory

384.s: Hutto explains he left Specht in fall 1924 because Specht left sidemen to lead the band, which Morehouse disliked.
384.ch: Bands, leaders and radio of the thirties and forties
384.q: I don't know why it broke up.

169.t: Back to Kirk, then Barnet's contract claim
169.s: He returns to Kirk, Barnet claims a contract, McGhee goes back, and quits in Detroit; his horn was stolen.
169.ch: Hampton, Andy Kirk and Charlie Barnet
169.q: '42. So I went back with Andy, and then like I said, Barnet called me and told me he had a contract and I had to fulfill the contract. So I went back with Barnet. But things kind of changed a little bit after that, you know, as far as Barnet and I were concerned. I liked him and everything, but I…

6.t: Quitting Henderson, disenchanted with the band
6.s: He gave two weeks notice because Henderson wasn't taking care of business and the band had declined.
6.q: I was totally, totally -- in other words, I was -- I can't think of the word, but anyway, I felt put down by Fletcher, because at that time he didn't take care of business, I'll put it that way. And so I quit. I just quit the band. You know, I wrote out my notice.

115.t: Leaving Vinson in St. Louis; Sil Austin's brother replaces him
115.s: He gave notice in San Francisco and left in St. Louis; a new drummer, Sil Austin's brother, lacked the swing.
115.ch: Postwar: Chicago, Vinson, Hines and Cootie
115.q: No, it wasn't the same thing at all, see. But Eddie hired him and he met him in St. Louis, and I let him sit in, play that date.

7.t: Leaving Cab: Greely Walton replaces him and he joins Don Redman
7.s: Having a job lined up, Thomas gives notice, Cab insists he find a replacement, and he finds Greely Walton before going with Redman.
7.q: This is way ahead of myself. But I got ready to leave. We was playing the Sheraton. I had made a deal to go... I'd already got me a gig. Because Jefferson always told me, he said, "Man, if you want a raise, always have somewhere to go if you can't get it and you're going to get fired."

529.t: Oscar Peterson's phone call and leaving Cannonball with Louis Hayes
529.s: Peterson phones Sam in Seattle at 5 a.m. to replace Ray Brown, Louis Hayes is also asked, and Sam takes double the pay.
529.q: You know, all they had to do was get another bass player you know, cause I was going to quit anyway and so uhm, we, out in California, no, we was out in Seattle, Washington somewhere in a hotel room, it was about 5:00 in the morning man, the phone, my phone rang you know.
